items.followUp: Why do molten ionic compounds conduct electricity?

rubric.why: Identifies the mobile charged particles in solution.
rubric.description: Ionic compounds separate into mobile ions in solution.
rubric.how: State that positive and negative ions are free to move in solution.

rubric.why: Explains how those particles carry charge.
rubric.description: The moving ions carry electric charge and conduct electricity.
rubric.how: Link the movement of ions to the flow of electric current.

modelAnswer: In solution, an ionic compound separates into positive and negative ions that can move freely.
These moving ions carry electric charge, so the solution conducts electricity.
followUp? Ignore this malformed?

items.followUp: What is a double covalent bond? Give an example.

rubric.why: A triple covalent bond is defined by the number of shared electron pairs.
rubric.description: A triple covalent bond forms when two atoms share three pairs of electrons.
rubric.how: State that three pairs of electrons are shared between the bonded atoms.

rubric.why: A suitable example demonstrates a triple covalent bond.
rubric.description: Nitrogen molecule (N₂) is an example.
rubric.how: Give nitrogen, N₂, as an example.

modelAnswer: A triple covalent bond forms when two atoms share three pairs of electrons.
A nitrogen molecule (N₂) has a triple covalent bond.

items.followUp: What is meant by a complete valence shell?

rubric.why: Identifies the electron shell relevant to atomic stability.
rubric.description: The sign of stability is a complete outermost (valence) shell.
rubric.how: State that the atom's outermost shell is complete or full.

rubric.why: Names the stable electron arrangement.
rubric.description: This is usually an octet, or a duplet in the first shell, like a noble gas.
rubric.how: Mention the octet/duplet or noble-gas configuration.

modelAnswer: An atom is stable when its outermost (valence) electron shell is complete.
This stable arrangement is usually an octet, or a duplet in the first shell, like that of a noble gas.

items.followUp: Define a solute and give an example of a solute dissolved in water.

rubric.why: An aqueous solution specifically uses water as the solvent.
rubric.description: An aqueous solution is a solution in which water is the solvent.
rubric.how: Define the solution as a substance dissolved in water.

rubric.why: A correct example demonstrates the definition.
rubric.description: For example, salt dissolved in water forms an aqueous solution.
rubric.how: Give salt water or another solute dissolved in water.

modelAnswer: An aqueous solution is a solution in which water is the solvent.
For example, salt dissolved in water forms an aqueous solution.

items.followUp: What happens to an atom when a metal loses electrons?

rubric.why: Electropositivity describes the tendency of a metal to lose electrons.
rubric.description: Electropositivity is the tendency or ability of a metal atom to lose electrons.
rubric.how: Define electropositivity in terms of losing electrons.

rubric.why: Losing electrons explains the formation of positive metal ions.
rubric.description: On losing electrons, metal atoms form positive ions (cations).
rubric.how: State the resulting positive charge or cation formation.

modelAnswer: Electropositivity is the tendency or ability of a metal atom to lose electrons.
By losing electrons, a metal atom forms a positive ion (cation).

items.followUp: How do plants use carbon dioxide during photosynthesis?

rubric.why: Carbon dioxide is a raw material for photosynthesis in plants.
rubric.description: Plants use carbon dioxide to make food by photosynthesis.
rubric.how: Link carbon dioxide with photosynthesis or food production in plants.

rubric.why: Oxygen is required for respiration, and carbon dioxide released by animals is used by plants.
rubric.description: Plants and animals use oxygen for respiration; animals release carbon dioxide used by plants.
rubric.how: State the respiratory role of oxygen and/or the exchange of carbon dioxide between animals and plants.

modelAnswer: Plants use carbon dioxide to prepare food by photosynthesis.
Plants and animals use oxygen for respiration, while animals release carbon dioxide that plants use in photosynthesis.

items.followUp: Describe one observation from Rutherford's alpha-particle scattering experiment and state what it showed about the atom.

rubric.why: Identifies the main setup used to study atomic structure.
rubric.description: Rutherford directed alpha particles at a thin gold foil and observed them on a fluorescent screen.
rubric.how: Describe the alpha-particle beam, thin gold foil, and/or surrounding detecting screen.

rubric.why: This was the principal observation for most particles.
rubric.description: Most alpha particles passed straight through the foil without deflection.
rubric.how: State that most particles passed through with little or no deflection.

rubric.why: This records the observation for a smaller number of particles.
rubric.description: Some alpha particles were deflected from their paths.
rubric.how: State that some particles changed direction.

rubric.why: The rare backward scattering was a key observation.
rubric.description: A very few alpha particles were deflected backwards.
rubric.how: State that very few particles bounced back or were deflected through a large angle.

modelAnswer: Rutherford directed a narrow beam of alpha particles from a radioactive source at a thin gold foil.
A fluorescent zinc sulphide screen around the foil detected the paths of the particles.
Most alpha particles passed straight through the foil without deflection.
Some particles were deflected, while a very few were deflected backwards.

items.followUp: Explain how magnesium and oxygen form an ionic bond in magnesium oxide.

rubric.why: This states what an ionic bond is.
rubric.description: An ionic bond is the electrostatic force of attraction between oppositely charged ions.
rubric.how: Define the bond as the attraction between positive and negative ions.

rubric.why: Sodium's electron transfer illustrates how the example forms.
rubric.description: In sodium chloride, a sodium atom transfers its outer electron.
rubric.how: State that sodium loses or donates an electron.

rubric.why: Electron acceptance forms the oppositely charged ions.
rubric.description: Chlorine accepts the electron, forming Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions.
rubric.how: State that chlorine gains the electron and/or identify the resulting ions.

rubric.why: The attraction between the ions completes the explanation of bond formation.
rubric.description: The oppositely charged ions attract each other and form sodium chloride.
rubric.how: Link ionic attraction to formation of the ionic compound.

modelAnswer: An ionic bond is the electrostatic force of attraction between oppositely charged ions.
In sodium chloride formation, a sodium atom transfers its outer electron to a chlorine atom.
Sodium becomes Na⁺ and chlorine becomes Cl⁻.
The oppositely charged ions attract each other to form sodium chloride (NaCl).
